extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, creative-writing students, and readers of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on creating, portraying, and integrating characters in the novel — how to reveal inner life, treat basic human experiences, choose flat vs round types, and balance character autonomy with narrative needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal the hidden life
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's function is to reveal the hidden life at its source — to tell us more about a person than history can know, producing characters who are not merely historical figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on inner experiences (dreams, joys, sorrows, self-communings) that politeness or shame would hide; expose the 'romanesque' side of human nature rather than just external actions. Use imagination to make secret life visible to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelistic method: thought developing into action (intentionality over fatality)
rubrics_metrics.description: In novels what matters is the method by which thought develops into action; unlike history, the novel's world is founded on human nature where events are intentional rather than ruled by fatality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray causation as stemming from character motivations and intentions. Avoid treating events as purely externally determined; show internal processes leading to actions to maintain novelistic plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial omniscience / complete character exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters in a novel can be understood completely by the reader if the novelist wishes; the novelist is allowed to remember and understand everything about a character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if not all facts are told, give the reader the impression that the narrator knows everything about the character so that the character feels explicable and 'real' within the book's world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters are real when convincing within the novel's laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A character is real not necessarily because it resembles daily life, but because it is convincing and lives in accordance with the novel's artistic laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that fiction has its own laws; prioritize internal coherence and convincingness over strict replication of everyday probabilities. The 'esthetic reply' — treat the novel as a work of art with its own requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of the five main human facts (birth, food, sleep, love, death)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist should examine how the basic facts of human life — birth, food, sleep, love and death — function in novels and whether they are reproduced, exaggerated, minimized or ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide deliberately how each basic human experience will be handled in the story, recognizing that novels often alter their proportion or significance for artistic purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of birth
rubrics_metrics.description: Birth in fiction is usually an experience known only by report and is seldom treated as a psychological experience; babies often appear 'posted' into novels and then kept until useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you choose to depict birth, be aware that few novelists attempt to reconstruct the baby's mind; consider whether to use birth as an explanatory device or to leave it unexplored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of death
rubrics_metrics.description: Death is congenial to the novelist: it ends a book neatly and the novelist can be both appropriate and imaginative about it by the time characters die.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use death as a structural and imaginative device, but avoid gratuitous or pseudo-seance attempts to report the 'life beyond'; draw on observation and character history to make deaths fitting and powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of food
rubrics_metrics.description: Food in fiction is mainly social: it draws characters together, but characters seldom require it physiologically and the aesthetic/sensuous side of eating is often neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting meals, use them to reveal social relations and character dynamics; consider whether to exploit the sensual, esthetic aspects of eating when it serves characterization or atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of sleep and dreams
rubrics_metrics.description: Sleep and dreams are frequently handled perfunctorily; dreams are introduced with purpose and are either logical or mosaic-like, not representing that a third of life occurs in sleep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If including dreams or sleep, ensure they serve a narrative or psychological purpose and avoid treating the dream-life as merely decorative; consider whether to attempt fuller reconstruction of dream experience or to use it instrumentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of love (broadly defined)
rubrics_metrics.description: Love dominates many novels — often excessively — becoming the chief concern of characters and causing monotony; its prevalence stems from the novelist's own sensitiveness and its utility as a convenient ending (marriage/ permanence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of over-emphasizing love to the exclusion of other human experiences; examine whether love in your novel exists for genuine character truth or out of authorial projection and narrative convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must adapt to plot and inter-dependencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters often must be fitted to other requirements of the novel — plot, moral stance, fellow characters, atmosphere — and in many works they are inter-dependent rather than isolated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design characters with their relationships and the plot's needs in mind; in closely woven novels (e.g., Austen) characters are bound to one another and cannot be plausibly removed or treated in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance character autonomy with authorial control
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are creations who may 'run away' or 'get out of hand' if given complete freedom, yet if kept too sternly in check they may 'die' or make the work inert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a productive tension: allow characters enough freedom to surprise and feel alive, but exercise sufficient control to preserve the integrity of plot and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of different kinds of characters (flat vs round)
rubrics_metrics.description: A key device for handling characters is to employ different kinds: flat characters (types/humours, constructed around a single idea) and round characters (complex, multiple facets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose flat characters when you need instant recognizability, economy, or permanence; choose round characters when you want development, psychological depth, and memorable change through scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages and limits of flat characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters can be expressed in one sentence, are immediately recognizable, never need reintroducing, do not 'run away', and help give a sense of permanence and easy memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use flat types as luminous, economical devices (supporting atmosphere or satire), but be mindful of critics who find them untrue to daily life; avoid using only flat characters where complexity is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages and nature of round characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters cannot be summed up in a single phrase; they are modified by circumstances and remembered through their scenes and development (e.g., Becky Sharp).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop round characters through incidents and changing situations so their multiplicity and growth feel authentic; accept that they may be harder for readers to reduce to a simple formula but richer in psychological truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view as a device for managing characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view (not elaborated in this excerpt) is named as a second major device, alongside character types, that novelists use to handle the problems of creating and integrating characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider choice of narrator/P.O.V. as a tool to reveal or conceal inner life, regulate the reader's knowledge of characters, and manage how characters fit the book's laws and plot requirements.
